extracted.intended_audience: MER organizers, program evaluators, mathematics department chairs, and mathematics educators interested in departmental- or network-level education reform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for assessing the effectiveness, design, and institutional impact of a mathematics education reform network (example: MER), including workshops, departmental networks, communications, and indicators of systemic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching as a tenure/promotion threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Decent teaching is a necessary but not sufficient condition for tenure and promotions; teaching that is much below par can block tenure/promotion even for candidates with solid research productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions require at least adequate teaching performance for tenure/promotion. Exceptional research may occasionally overcome poor teaching, but generally teaching must meet departmental standards. Use this as a baseline criterion when evaluating faculty reward structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research as primary promotion focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary focus in the departments studied remains research; educational work alone will not typically secure promotion to full professor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing departmental incentives, evaluate how strongly research output is weighted relative to educational contributions and whether educational work is explicitly recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional rewards and supports for educational work
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained educational reform requires changes in institutional reward structures, e.g., consideration of educational activities in promotion/tenure decisions, release time, administrative support, and respect for educational involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for explicit policies (promotion criteria, release time, administrative recognition). Examples: some departments reported expanded consideration of educational endeavors; others lacked institutional supports making initiatives precarious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of internal champions/liaisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments with at least one faculty member strongly tied to MER (Advisory Board member, co-director, or active participant) gave MER instant credibility and drove departmental engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether there are identifiable local advocates who can translate network activity into departmental action. Lack of champions makes initiatives vulnerable if those individuals leave (e.g., Penn State example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership involvement (department chairs and administrators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requesting that the department chair attend the first meeting was an important strategic move to increase likelihood of broad departmental acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate network strategies for engaging decision-makers; presence of chairs at workshops and tailored sessions for administrators increases chance of department-level change and resource leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of faculty awareness and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of MER was variable: generally less than half of faculty had heard of MER and fewer than one-quarter understood the implications of their department's relationship with the Forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure both awareness and depth of understanding across faculty. Low awareness suggests need for broader communication strategies and targeted outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop design features that maximize outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality workshops had an overarching theme, breakout sessions for specific interests, and substantial informal contact time (meals, hallway conversations) which fostered trust and idea exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating workshops, look for theme coherence, opportunities for small-group focus, and built-in informal interaction. The report emphasizes face-to-face formats for creating unplanned, fruitful interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-to-face interaction value vs remote modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Face-to-face exchanges (including informal 'hallway' conversations) were repeatedly cited as the most valuable aspect of workshops; some benefits are unlikely to be replicated remotely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether in-person formats are justified by outcomes that cannot be achieved via written materials or remote communication. Consider hybrid approaches where appropriate, but value in-person for networking and spontaneous idea generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop outcomes: validation and modest novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops often validated participants' existing ideas and introduced educational concepts that, while not cutting-edge for the field, were new to many mathematicians (e.g., NCTM Standards, cooperative learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate impact in terms of participants' reported intentions to incorporate workshop ideas and whether workshops provide credible, actionable practices rather than purely theoretical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental network as accelerator of systemic change
rubrics_metrics.description: The departmental network (teams from departments, chairs involved) was seen as a quicker path toward systemic reform than the individual network because key decision-makers and groups can press central administration for favorable policies/resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether network activities involve multiple members per department and whether they engage administrative decision-makers; such involvement increases probability of department-level policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of systemic reform (per Jenness & Barley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systemic reform should be judged by whether the network encourages development of new working relationships within the mathematics community and among related disciplines, and whether broad changes have occurred beyond local/individual changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metrics for new inter-unit collaborations, cross-disciplinary initiatives, and measurable shifts in departmental practices or policies as evidence of systemic reform. Distinguish individual-level improvements from system-level changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common individual-level impact metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Three common types of individual changes reported: (1) enhanced awareness of educational issues, (2) strengthened feelings of support, and (3) improved classroom pedagogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measurement of these three dimensions in evaluations (surveys, interviews, classroom observation) to capture the network's individual-level effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability and institutionalization of initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: K-12 and other educational activities often rest on very few faculty members; without broader departmental/institutional support these initiatives are precarious and likely to falter if key individuals leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess distribution of responsibilities, formalization of programs, and backup structures; successful institutionalization involves multiple stakeholders and embedding activities in departmental structures (example: UT-Austin had a mathematics educator on faculty and stronger institutional support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeding inter-departmental collaboration and projects
rubrics_metrics.description: The network facilitated collaborative projects (e.g., planning grants, interdisciplinary initiatives), graduate/postdoc exchanges, internships, and sharing of curricular projects arising from workshop interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track whether workshops produce concrete collaborative plans, follow-up commitments (grants, exchanges), and resource-sharing arrangements among departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimization effect within research community
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing concrete examples of what other mathematicians are doing in educational reform helps legitimize educational interests within the mathematics research community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether network activities change perceptions among research-focused faculty by documenting shifts in rhetoric, acceptance, and willingness to support education work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication strategy: moderated vs open listserver
rubrics_metrics.description: Original plan limited listserver subscriptions to a few faculty who would moderate and forward; the evaluators suggest opening the listserver to any interested individual to reduce burden on liaisons and increase participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess trade-offs between preventing information overload and encouraging wide participation. Monitor listserver traffic and consider opening subscription if low traffic indicates little risk of flooding inboxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of skeptical participants to build credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some departments invited 'cynics' to workshops to provide credibility when reporting back to colleagues; this tactic can help demonstrate efficacy to skeptical audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning workshops, consider deliberately inviting skeptical or resistant faculty to increase internal credibility of reported outcomes and ease uptake upon return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness vs unique benefits of in-person events
rubrics_metrics.description: Although workshops are resource-intensive, face-to-face contact yielded unique benefits (networking, unplanned interactions) that the evaluators judged worth the investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cost-benefit analyses that account for qualitative networking outcomes and long-term capacity-building when deciding to fund in-person events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology: broaden target group and trace indirect effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective evaluation included interviewing both participants and non-participants, tracing indirect MER influences, and seeking subtle communication patterns to avoid underestimating effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluations to capture both direct and indirect impacts: include diverse informants, longitudinal follow-up, and methods to trace information diffusion beyond formal participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of shared resources/databases to leverage change
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing a database to provide comparative information for department chairs and others was proposed as a leverage tool (e.g., to address declining majors by sharing institutional responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess potential for centralized data resources to support departments' requests for resources and provide quick comparative benchmarks; track usage and relevance of such databases.
